input:
Case
At present, the plant discharges treated water that fully meets its consent conditions, while at the same time drawing fresh water for a range of duties that do not actually require fresh-water quality. The case for the proposed recycling plant rests on the gap between these two positions: washdown, floor washing, and utility make-up duties on the site can all accept recycled water of the quality that the treatment step already produces, and every unit volume that is recycled is a unit volume that is neither drawn nor discharged. The proposal takes the duties in order of the quality that each of them accepts, beginning with the duties that are furthest from any product contact, and it establishes a quality boundary that no recycled stream is permitted to cross towards product use. This boundary is a fundamental design rule of the scheme rather than a mere operating preference, and the pipework has been arranged so that the boundary is held by the physical layout itself rather than by procedural controls.

The need for the scheme stands on the site's own water balance: both the draw and the discharge are metered, and the duties identified above represent the measured share of the draw that the recycled quality is able to satisfy. Recycling will not change production, product quality, or the consent position; what it changes is the source of the utility water and the volume that is discharged. The alternative of leaving the current arrangement entirely as it stands would retain the full draw and the full discharge, and the case has been stated against that alternative.

The duties that have been named are continuous duties rather than campaign duties, so the recycled volume is essentially a steady volume rather than an intermittent one, and the plant has been sized on the steady demand, with the collection tank absorbing the mismatch between the treatment output and the draw of the duties over the course of the day. A scheme sized on peak demand would carry tank and treatment capacity that stands idle for most of the day, whereas a scheme sized on the steady demand with storage represents the cheaper arrangement, and it is the arrangement proposed here. The quality that the treatment step produces is already monitored at the discharge under the consent sampling regime, so the quality claim behind the case rests on measurements that the site already takes and reports, rather than on any new characterisation carried out specially for this proposal.

Costs
The capital cost of the scheme is $1346k, appraised over a 10-year horizon. The capital figure covers the collection tank, the treatment top-up that the recycled quality requires, the distribution pipework to the duties named in the case, and the controls that serve to hold the quality boundary. Operating cost consists of pumping, treatment consumables, and the sampling that the boundary requires; the sampling regime forms part of the design rather than an addition to it, on the grounds that an unmonitored boundary is not really a boundary at all. Savings arise from the avoided draw and the avoided discharge charges on the recycled volume, taken at the tariffs in force at the time of appraisal and held flat over the horizon, so that the appraisal does not depend on any assumption of tariff escalation. Maintenance has been carried as a cost line at the rate that the site applies to utility plant of this class.

The appraisal has been stated on those terms and no others: no value has been taken for water security, for consent headroom, or for any future tightening of the discharge terms, even though each of these may well follow from the scheme. A case that needs those items in order to stand would be a weaker case than the one presented here, and they have accordingly been recorded as unvalued consequences rather than as benefits within the appraisal.

The capital figure is an estimate at proposal stage, built up from vendor quotations for the tank and the treatment package and from site rates for the pipework and the controls. It carries the estimating allowance that the site applies at this stage and no more than that; the detailed design stage exists in order to replace the estimate with a properly priced scope, and the construction appraisal will be made on that priced scope rather than on the figure given here. The sensitivity also runs in the other direction: the savings depend on the recycled volume, and the volume depends on the duties retaining their present level of demand. A duty that closes, or that converts back to fresh water for process reasons, will reduce both the recycled volume and the savings, while the capital and the fixed operating costs remain in place, and that exposure forms part of the case on which the decision is taken.

Schedule
Work will start one quarter after approval has been given. The sequence runs from the collection tank and the treatment top-up, which together fix the quality that the scheme can offer, through to the distribution pipework, which is laid duty by duty so that each individual duty transfers to recycled water as its branch is completed and proven. Tie-ins to live services will be made during planned outages, and the schedule carries the outage windows as firm constraints rather than as float. Commissioning proceeds duty by duty in exactly the same order: a duty transfers only after the recycled supply to that duty has held its quality through the sampling regime, and any duty that fails sampling remains on fresh water until the cause has been found and corrected. No contractor has been named in this proposal; the executing contractor will be selected under the site procurement route following approval, and the schedule has been written in such a way that the selection does not alter the sequence.

The long-lead items are the tank and the treatment package, and procurement of these items will start on the construction decision rather than on the design approval sought here, so the design stage does not sit on the critical path of the equipment. Pipework installation is the activity that touches the operating plant most directly, and it has been phased so that no duty loses its water supply at any point during the works: each branch is completed and pressure-tested alongside the live main before its tie-in outage, and the tie-in itself is the only step that actually requires the outage. The schedule sets out the sequence and the constraints; the detailed durations will be fixed at the detailed design stage, when the routes and the outage calendar for the construction period are fully known.

Decision requested
The decision that is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and not to construction. Detailed design will fix the tank size, the treatment duty, and the pipework routes against a proper site survey, and it will return a construction cost and a construction schedule on the basis of which a separate construction decision can subsequently be taken. Approval at this stage commits the design cost only. The construction decision, supported by its own appraisal on the detailed figures, will come back to the same body that is being asked to approve the design stage here.
